# Should I swap my gas boiler for a heat pump?

*Typical English 3-bed semi on the Ofgem price cap (Oct-Dec 2026). Prices and efficiency come from the sources at the bottom; everything else is a flagged assumption. Every figure below is generated by `heatpump_model.py`, so you can change an input and regenerate the file (see 'Re-run it').*

## The answer

> **Verdict: NO on a standard tariff; TOO CLOSE on a heat-pump tariff**  
> **Confidence: High (on a standard tariff the simulation agrees with this in 95% of 5,000 draws)**

- **Bottom line:** don't do it just to save money on a standard tariff. On a heat-pump tariff it roughly breaks even, so it comes down to the efficiency your installer predicts and whether you value the non-financial benefits.
- **Over 15 years, a heat pump on a standard tariff leaves you £3,077 worse off than keeping a gas boiler** (£3,932 worse off in today's money). On a heat-pump tariff you'd be £46 worse off (£1,649 worse off in today's money).
- **Running costs barely differ; the up-front cost is what decides it.** In year 1 the heat pump's bills are £71 lower on a standard tariff or £234 lower on a heat-pump tariff, but you pay £7,500 after the grant. Keeping the boiler means paying £3,000 for a new one in year 5, which narrows the gap but doesn't close it.
- **Why bills are so similar:** a kWh of heat costs about 9.4p from your gas boiler and 8.8p from a heat pump at SCOP 3.0 on the standard tariff. Electricity costs 3.3x as much per kWh as gas, which cancels out most of the heat pump's efficiency.

### What would flip it

| If... | Today's assumption | The heat pump breaks even over the period when... |
|---|---|---|
| Your installer's **predicted SCOP** (efficiency) is higher | 3.0 | 3.97 on a standard tariff, 3.01 on a heat-pump tariff |
| You get a **cheaper electricity tariff** for heating | 26.3p standard; 20p assumed heat-pump tariff | 19.9p/kWh blended or lower, at SCOP 3.0 |
| The **installed price** is lower | £7,500 | £4,423 (standard tariff) or £7,454 (heat-pump tariff) |
| Your home uses more **gas** | 9,500 kWh/yr | no realistic level (standard tariff), 9,618 kWh/yr (heat-pump tariff) |
| Your **boiler is failing soon** | replaced in year 5 | see the 'when the boiler would need replacing' row in the drivers table |

The simulation below says the three things that move the result most are: heat pump efficiency, fuel price paths, and heat-pump tariff blended price. Of all the inputs, efficiency and tariff price can be pinned down before you buy; future fuel prices can't.

Rule of thumb: ask installers for a written heat-loss calculation and a predicted SCOP. If it is below the SCOP in the first row, the heat pump is unlikely to pay back on running costs alone.

## The 15-year picture

Total cash spent from today (heat pump installed now vs. keeping the boiler and replacing it in year 5). Prices rise each year as set in the assumptions. A positive 'heat pump ahead by' means the heat pump has cost less in total.

| Year | Keep boiler: total spent | Heat pump (standard tariff): total spent | Heat pump ahead by | Heat pump (heat-pump tariff): total spent | Heat pump ahead by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | £0 | £7,500 | -£7,500 | £7,500 | -£7,500 |
| 1 | £965 | £8,394 | -£7,429 | £8,231 | -£7,266 |
| 2 | £1,957 | £9,311 | -£7,354 | £8,980 | -£7,023 |
| 3 | £2,975 | £10,251 | -£7,276 | £9,747 | -£6,772 |
| 5 | £8,095 | £12,202 | -£4,107 | £11,337 | -£3,242 |
| 7 | £10,274 | £14,254 | -£3,981 | £13,005 | -£2,732 |
| 10 | £13,770 | £17,534 | -£3,764 | £15,666 | -£1,896 |
| 12 | £16,263 | £19,865 | -£3,601 | £17,552 | -£1,289 |
| 15 | £19,268 | £22,345 | -£3,077 | £19,315 | -£46 |

The heat pump starts £7,500 behind and claws it back through lower bills. Standard tariff: never breaks even within 15 years. Heat-pump tariff: never breaks even within 15 years. The step in the 'keep boiler' column at year 5 is the replacement boiler. Remaining life of each system at the end is credited at what you paid, spread evenly over its lifespan (a notional value, not a sale price).

## How well does the answer hold up?

**Simulation.** I varied every uncertain input at once (5,000 random draws around your inputs: efficiency, gas use, installed price, boiler age and cost, fuel price rises, tariff price, whether VAT returns). The ranges are my judgement, centred on the base case and spelled out in `monte_carlo()`; they are not measured spreads.

| | Heat pump cheaper in... | Typical result (median) | 80% of draws fall between |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standard tariff | 5% of draws | -£3,336 | -£6,187 to -£675 |
| Heat-pump tariff | 41% of draws | -£484 | -£3,264 to +£2,298 |

**What matters most.** Each row moves one input between plausible extremes and shows the heat pump's advantage at each end (positive = heat pump ahead after the full period). Rows are ranked by how far they move the result.

| Input (extremes tested) | Standard tariff | Heat-pump tariff |
|---|---|---|
| Heat pump efficiency (SCOP 2.6 to 4.0) | -£5,019 to +£78 | -£1,522 to +£2,351 |
| Fuel price paths (elec dearer: gas +2%/elec +4% to elec cheaper: gas +4%/elec +2%) | -£5,238 to -£905 | -£1,975 to +£1,913 |
| Heat-pump tariff blended price (25p to 16p; heat-pump tariff only) | -£3,077 to -£3,077 | -£2,444 to +£1,872 |
| When the boiler would need replacing (never in period to now) | -£4,748 to -£2,208 | -£1,718 to +£823 |
| Net installed price (£9,000 to £6,000) | -£4,327 to -£1,827 | -£1,296 to +£1,204 |
| Home's gas use (7,500 to 12,000 kWh/yr) | -£3,195 to -£2,929 | -£831 to +£935 |
| Replacement boiler cost (£2,200 to £4,500) | -£3,610 to -£2,077 | -£580 to +£954 |
| Keep gas connected (yes to no) | -£4,461 to -£3,077 | -£1,430 to -£46 |
| VAT on electricity (5% to 0%) | -£3,769 to -£3,077 | -£587 to -£46 |
| Existing boiler efficiency (90% to 78%) | -£3,272 to -£2,804 | -£63 to -£23 |

**Self-test.** The model must reproduce numbers it didn't make up:

- Pass: Ofgem typical bill reproduced within £1 (£1,724 vs £1,723)
- Pass: Nesta running-cost parity (ratio 3.3, efficiency 2.8, boiler 85%; Nesta rounds, so within 1%) (boiler £950 vs heat pump £952)
- Pass: Hand-derived flat-price case (model +£1,000 vs by hand +£1,000)
- Pass: Higher efficiency never hurts

## Assumptions and sources

`SOURCE` = taken from a cited source (some figures are still estimates). `ASSUMPTION` = my estimate; replace it if you know better.

| Input | Value | Type | Note |
|---|---|---|---|

| ...of which gas cooking (kWh) | 400 | ASSUMPTION | Rest is heating + hot water. |
| Electricity for cooking if gas is disconnected (kWh) | 250 | ASSUMPTION | Induction hob/oven. |
| Existing boiler real-world efficiency | 85% | ASSUMPTION | Older condensing boiler. |
| Replacement boiler real-world efficiency | 88% | ASSUMPTION | New condensing boiler. |
| Gas unit price (GBP/kWh) | 0.0797 | SOURCE | Ofgem cap, Oct-Dec 2026, incl. 5% VAT. |
| Gas standing charge (GBP/day) | 0.2968 | SOURCE | Ofgem cap, Oct-Dec 2026. |
| Electricity unit price (GBP/kWh) | 0.2632 | SOURCE | Ofgem cap, Oct-Dec 2026, no VAT currently. |
| VAT added to electricity (fraction) | 0.0 | ASSUMPTION | 0 = as published. Ofgem lists no VAT on electricity for Oct 2026-Mar 2027; I could not confirm what happens after. See sensitivity table. |
| Heat pump seasonal efficiency (SCOP/SPF) | 3.0 | ASSUMPTION | Field trial median 2.8 (older installs); Nesta models 3.0. No survey of your house yet. |
| Blended price on a heat-pump tariff (GBP/kWh) | 0.20 | ASSUMPTION | Octopus Cosy-style: ~13p cheap, ~26p day, ~39p peak, weighted by when heat pumps run. |
| Heat pump net cost after grant (GBP) | 7,500 | SOURCE | Your figure; Boiler Upgrade Scheme is up to GBP 7,500. |
| Heat pump annual service (GBP) | 150 | ASSUMPTION |  |
| Boiler annual service (GBP) | 100 | ASSUMPTION |  |
| Year existing boiler would be replaced | 5 | ASSUMPTION | Boiler assumed ~10 years old with a ~15 year life. 0 = it is dying now. |
| New boiler installed cost (GBP) | 3,000 | ASSUMPTION |  |
| Boiler lifespan (years) | 15 | ASSUMPTION | Used to credit remaining life at the end of the period. |
| Heat pump lifespan (years) | 18 | ASSUMPTION | Typically quoted as 15-20 years. |
| Years compared | 15 | ASSUMPTION |  |
| Gas price rise per year | 3.00% | ASSUMPTION | Both fuels rise together in the base case. |
| Electricity price rise per year | 3.00% | ASSUMPTION |  |
| Discount rate for 'today's money' view | 3.50% | ASSUMPTION | HM Treasury Green Book rate. |
| Disconnect gas when heat pump goes in (1=yes, 0=no) | 1 | ASSUMPTION |  |

**Sources and how far to trust them**

- Price cap: [Ofgem unit rates and standing charges](https://www.ofgem.gov.uk/node/176588/), average Direct Debit, Oct-Dec 2026 (electricity 26.32p/kWh + 54.83p/day; gas 7.97p/kWh + 29.68p/day). Official. These are averages across England, Scotland and Wales, not England-only, and the price cap changes every quarter.
- Typical use (9,500 kWh gas, 2,500 kWh electricity): Ofgem's 2026 review, as reported by [Energy UK](https://www.energy-uk.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Energy-UK-Explains-Typical-Domestic-Consumption-Values.pdf). I could not open Ofgem's own decision page, but these figures with the cap prices reproduce Ofgem's £1,723 typical bill to within £1 (see the check in the script output).
- Heat pump efficiency: [Electrification of Heat trial](https://es.catapult.org.uk/news/heat-pumps-shown-to-be-three-times-more-efficient-than-gas-boilers/) (Energy Systems Catapult), median seasonal efficiency 2.8 for air-source heat pumps. These are interim results from the 742-home trial; I did not find the final report. [Nesta](https://www.nesta.org.uk/report/how-to-make-heat-pumps-more-affordable/assumptions-and-methods/) assumes 3.0, and its modelling also finds heat pumps unlikely to cut bills for most households at today's price ratio. [Carbon Brief](https://www.carbonbrief.org/factcheck-what-it-really-costs-to-heat-a-home-in-the-uk-with-a-heat-pump) notes that the Heat Pump Monitor site shows about 3.9, but that site covers self-selected, often enthusiast, owners, so I did not use it as the typical case.
- Grant: [GOV.UK, Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/heat-pump-grants-increased-by-50-per-cent): up to £7,500 for an air-source heat pump in England and Wales. I did not confirm the scheme's end date; check GOV.UK before relying on it. The £7,500 net cost is your figure.
- Heat-pump tariff: Octopus [publishes average Cosy rates](https://octopus.energy/press/Octopus-Energy-launches-new-off-peak-rate-for-heat-pump-customers/) (cheap about 13p, day about 26p, peak about 40p). My 20p blended price is my own weighting of those, and current rates vary by region. Check live rates before relying on it.
- Not sourced at all: boiler and heat pump lifetimes, replacement boiler cost, service costs, future price rises.

## Plain-English glossary

- **SCOP / seasonal efficiency:** units of heat delivered per unit of electricity over a year. 3.0 means 1 kWh of electricity gives 3 kWh of heat. A gas boiler delivers about 0.85-0.9 kWh of heat per kWh of gas.
- **kWh:** the unit your meter and bills use for energy.
- **Standing charge:** a fixed daily fee for being connected. If you disconnect gas completely you stop paying the gas one, which is worth roughly £108 a year; the electricity one stays.
- **Price cap:** Ofgem's limit on the unit rates and standing charges suppliers can charge on standard tariffs. It is not a limit on your total bill.
- **Boiler Upgrade Scheme:** a government grant that comes off the installer's price.
- **Heat-pump tariff:** electricity that is cheap at certain times of day. It only helps if your heat pump and hot-water heating can run mostly in the cheap windows.
- **Today's money:** future savings reduced slightly because £100 later is worth less than £100 now.

## Limits

- This is a model with typical inputs, not a survey of your house. A proper heat-loss calculation from an installer will replace my efficiency assumption.
- Not counted: higher home value, carbon savings, any radiator or pipework upgrades beyond the net price you gave, installation disruption, extra running cost of a hot-water cylinder, solar panels, and what happens if the grant ends.
- Electricity standing charge is the same in both cases, so it's left out.

## Re-run it

```
python3 heatpump_model.py --list                          # see every input
python3 heatpump_model.py --set gas_kwh=12000 --set scop=3.4   # try your own numbers
python3 heatpump_model.py --set gas_kwh=12000 --write heat-pump-vs-gas-boiler.md   # regenerate this file
python3 heatpump_model.py --check heat-pump-vs-gas-boiler.md   # confirm the file matches the model
```
